title: I Wouldn't Buy the Anthropic IPO
body:
My problem with Anthropic's IPO is the price. I can believe Claude will become more useful, that businesses will spend heavily on it, and that Anthropic will grow into a huge company. I still struggle to see why I should buy shares at a valuation approaching $2 trillion.
At that price, an awful lot has to go right.
The growth is impressive. But investors are buying what comes next, and the expectations leave little room for an ordinary bad quarter. A slowdown that would be perfectly manageable for the business could be brutal for the share price.
Then there's the cost of staying competitive. Anthropic has to keep spending on computing power and development while rivals try to win the same customers. Being ahead today offers little comfort if defending that position keeps getting more expensive.
I'm also sceptical of the assumption that businesses will become permanently loyal to one AI provider. They have every reason to compare prices, use several services and switch when something better comes along. That makes future profits harder to predict than the excitement suggests.
The shares might jump on their first day. I wouldn't be surprised. A heavily anticipated listing can attract plenty of buyers before anyone starts asking difficult questions.
My bet is that the disappointment comes later, when strong results turn out to be insufficient to justify the price people paid.
I like the product. I wouldn't buy the IPO.

levels.headline: Why Wilf Brown would not buy Anthropic shares
levels.body:
Wilf Brown, a member of the Polinomics crew, says he would not buy shares in the Anthropic IPO because of the price. He believes Claude will get more useful, that businesses will spend a lot on it and that Anthropic will become a very large company. His doubt is about paying a valuation close to $2 trillion for it.
In his view, the growth is impressive but investors are paying for what comes next. Expectations are so high that even an ordinary bad quarter could hurt. A slowdown the business could cope with might still cause a painful fall in the share price.
He adds that staying competitive is expensive. Anthropic must keep paying for computing power and new development while rivals chase the same customers. He also doubts that firms will remain loyal to a single AI provider, since they can compare prices, use several services and switch, so future profits are hard to forecast.
He thinks the shares may rise on the first day, as a much-discussed listing can draw plenty of buyers before tougher questions are asked. He expects disappointment later, when good results are not good enough to justify the price. He likes the product but would stay away from the IPO.
levels.why: It shows how a good company can still be a risky investment if the price already assumes everything goes well.

levels.headline: Wilf Brown says Anthropic's IPO price is too high
levels.body:
Wilf Brown, writing for Polinomics, says he would not buy shares when Anthropic floats on the stock market. The company is making a product he likes, and he thinks it will grow. His objection is that shares are priced at a valuation approaching $2 trillion, which he finds hard to justify.
He says investors buy shares for what a firm might do in future, not only for what it has done. When hopes are this high, there is little room for a merely ordinary bad quarter. A slowdown that the business could handle might hit the share price hard.
Costs are another worry. To stay ahead, Anthropic has to keep spending on computing power and development while rivals try to win the same customers. Being ahead now means little if staying ahead keeps getting dearer. He also doubts that businesses will stay faithful to one AI provider, because they can compare prices, use several and switch, which makes profits harder to predict.
He accepts the shares could rise sharply on day one, since a widely expected listing can attract buyers before people ask hard questions. He believes the letdown will come later. He likes the product, but not the price.
levels.why: It asks readers to separate a firm's quality from the price they would pay for a share in it.

levels.headline: Columnist would not buy Anthropic shares at the IPO price

He says the company's growth is impressive, yet buyers are paying for the future. Expectations are so high that one ordinary bad quarter could cause trouble. A slowdown that is fine for the business could be harsh for the share price.

He is also doubtful that firms will stay loyal to one AI provider. They can compare prices, use more than one service and move when something better appears, so future profits are hard to predict.

levels.headline: Writer says Anthropic shares will cost too much
levels.body:
Wilf Brown is a writer for Polinomics. He says he would not buy shares in Anthropic. Anthropic is the company that makes Claude, an AI helper. Soon it will sell shares to the public for the first time. This is called an IPO. Wilf likes Claude and thinks the company will grow very big. But the price is too high for him. The company would be worth nearly $2 trillion.
Wilf says the company is growing fast. But buyers pay for what may happen later. People expect so much that even one normal bad quarter, which is three months of weaker sales, could cause trouble. The business might be fine, but the share price could fall hard.
Staying ahead costs a lot too. Anthropic must keep paying for computer power and new work. Other firms want the same customers. Wilf also thinks businesses may not stay loyal. They can check prices, use more than one AI service, and switch if something is better. That makes profits hard to guess.
He thinks the shares may go up on the first day, because many people will want them. But he thinks people may be let down later. He likes the product. He would not buy the IPO.
levels.why: It teaches that what you pay for something matters as much as how good it is.

levels.headline: Why a writer would not buy shares in a big AI firm
levels.body:
Wilf Brown writes for Polinomics. He says he would not buy shares in a company called Anthropic. It makes an AI helper called Claude. Soon the company will sell shares to people for the first time. This is called an IPO. A share is a small piece of a company. Wilf likes Claude. He thinks the company will get big. But the price is very high. It is worth nearly $2 trillion.
Wilf says the company is growing fast. But people who buy shares are paying for what might happen next. They hope for a lot. So even a normal bad few months could cause problems. The company could be fine, but the price of its shares could fall a lot.
It also costs a lot to stay ahead. The company must keep paying for computer power. Other firms want its customers. Wilf thinks businesses may not stay loyal. They can compare prices and switch. That makes it hard to know how much money the company will make.
He thinks the shares might rise on day one, as many people will want them. But he thinks they may be let down later. He likes the product. He would not buy the IPO.
levels.why: It shows that a good company can still cost too much to buy into.

levels.headline: A writer says a big AI company costs too much to buy
levels.body:
A writer called Wilf Brown says he would not buy a piece of a company called Anthropic. Anthropic makes Claude, a computer helper. The company will soon sell small pieces of itself, called shares, to the public. This is called an IPO. Wilf likes Claude. He thinks Anthropic will grow big. But he thinks the price is too high.
The company is growing fast. But people who buy shares are paying for the future. They are hoping for lots of good things. So if the company has even a normal bad few months, its share price could drop a lot. The company could still be doing fine.
It also costs a lot to stay the best. Anthropic needs to pay for strong computers. Other companies want its customers too. Wilf thinks customers might not stay. They can look at prices and switch to something better. So it is hard to know how much money the company will make.
Wilf thinks the shares might go up on the first day, because many people want them. But he thinks people may feel let down later. He likes the product. He would not buy the shares.
levels.why: It shows that something can be good and still cost too much.

levels.headline: Why Wilf would not buy a share in the Claude company
levels.body:
Wilf is a writer. He says he would not buy a share in the company that makes Claude. A share is a tiny piece of a company. Soon, people will be able to buy pieces of this company for the first time. Wilf likes Claude. He thinks the company will grow big. But he thinks the price is too high. It is like paying a huge amount for a sweet shop that has not sold much yet.
Lots of people expect the company to do very well. But if it does only okay for a little while, the price of its pieces could drop a lot. Think of a football team that is expected to win every game. One draw can make everyone sad.
The company also has to spend lots of money to stay the best. Other companies want to win its customers. Customers can also change to a different company if it is better, like picking a new playground game.
Wilf thinks the price might go up on the first day, because many people will want a piece. But he thinks people may feel let down later. He likes Claude. He would not buy a share.
levels.why: It shows that even a great thing can cost too much, like sweets that are priced far above their worth.

body: Burnham at the Labour conference announced the triple lock was coming to an end, broke down in tears over his dad, and spoke to the media about the Man City charges. He thinks that man city have been good for English football, and that the owners have contributed well to the local economy.

levels.body:
At the Labour party conference, Andy Burnham announced that the triple lock was coming to an end. During his appearance he broke down in tears while speaking about his father, a moment that visibly moved those watching.

Burnham also addressed the media on the ongoing charges against Manchester City. He gave his view that the club has been good for English football more broadly, strengthening the game's profile and competitiveness.

He further argued that City's owners have made a positive contribution to the local economy around Manchester, pointing to their wider investment in the city beyond football itself.

Taken together, the conference appearance combined a significant policy announcement with a personal, emotional moment and a defence of a club facing serious allegations.
levels.headline: Burnham announces end of the triple lock amid emotional conference moment
levels.why: It matters because a major policy change was announced alongside a public figure's personal defence of a football club under investigation.

levels.body:

He went further, saying Manchester City's owners have contributed well to the local economy, suggesting their investment has benefited the area beyond just the football club.

The conference therefore saw Burnham mix a notable policy statement with a personal moment and comments defending a club currently under scrutiny over serious allegations.

levels.why: It matters because it shows a senior figure announcing policy change while also publicly backing a club facing charges.

levels.body:
At a big Labour party meeting, Andy Burnham said a rule called the triple lock would stop. While talking, he got upset and cried about his father.

He also talked to reporters about problems Manchester City are having, called charges. Burnham said he thinks the club has been good for football in England.

levels.headline: Burnham ends a key promise, cries about his dad at a big meeting
levels.why: It matters because rule changes and support for a club in trouble can affect lots of people, like changing a school rule everyone relies on.

levels.body:
Imagine a school where everyone has a special rule that protects them, like always getting extra pocket money on your birthday. Andy Burnham told a big Labour meeting that a rule like this, called the triple lock, was going to stop.

While he was talking, he got sad and cried, because he was thinking about his dad.

He then talked to reporters about Manchester City, a football club in trouble for breaking rules, called charges. Burnham said he thinks the club has actually been good for football, like a popular team that makes everyone excited.

He said the owners also helped the area around the club, bringing jobs and money, like a shop owner who helps the whole street do well.
levels.headline: Burnham's big day: a rule ends, a tear, and a football team defended
levels.why: It matters because when a protective rule ends, and someone defends a team in trouble, it can change things for lots of people, a bit like changing a rule everyone in school depends on.
